claims.text: TypeSafe AI opened early access to Jev, their SystemOne model, in the week before this post was published (September 2026).
Jev is TypeSafe AI's SystemOne model.
TypeSafe's Jev provides AI primitives that let apps, agents, and workflows make decisions based on context, including confidence scoring, multiple choice, and yes/no (noul) questions.
Jev's decision-making primitives are confidence scoring, multiple choice, and yes/no (noul) questions.
Jev's decision-making primitives are the perfect complement to agentic work.
Combining Jev's reasoning with Pulumi makes the gap between designing ideal infrastructure and deploying it to production practically vanish.
In the past, having more infrastructure choices usually meant more complexity and technical debt; now agents can handle provisioning and day-to-day scaling and reliability decisions.

GeoDeploy is a Pulumi example (github.com/pulumi/devx-geodeploy) that takes target geos, an image, and a workload shape, decides where the workload should run and what it will cost, and then provisions it.

A GeoDeploy deployment request has four parts: target geos (traffic share and data-residency rule of EU-only, US-only, or in-country), a container image with platforms (amd64, arm64, or both), a workload shape (replicas, CPU and memory per pod, egress, storage), and constraints (allowed providers, max number of providers, budget).
GeoDeploy compares every AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud region that offers managed Kubernetes, picks the best one for each geo, and provisions consistent environments across all three hyperscalers.

In GeoDeploy's design, the TypeScript app takes the request, fetches live pricing, and does all the math but makes no judgment calls; Jev decides which region wins and which modules to use but does no arithmetic, code generation, or region-name invention; Pulumi provisions clusters, registries, workloads, and DNS but decides nothing.
GeoDeploy's first pipeline step maps each business region (geo) to a canonical location and residency class.
GeoDeploy lists every region with managed Kubernetes and uses great-circle distance as a coverage measure.
GeoDeploy fetches current prices from the AWS Price List API, the Azure Retail Prices API, and the Google Cloud Billing Catalog, normalized into a single quote format.
GeoDeploy uses deterministic TypeScript to bin-pack pods onto nodes, filter out instance types that don't match the image's architecture, and compute a monthly cost for each candidate.
GeoDeploy composes a Pulumi program from a curated registry of typed modules: EKS, AKS, or GKE; ECR, ACR, or Artifact Registry; ingress; DNS through Route 53, NS1, or Cloudflare; and observability.
GeoDeploy uses the Pulumi Automation API to run a preview and then an update, with one stack per region, and will not run unless cloud credentials pass readiness checks.
The link /automation/ is a valid Pulumi site page for the Automation API.
Every GeoDeploy run writes a plan.json and plan.md with the full decision record, and a web UI shows the deployment on a live globe.
Jev returns typed answers with calibrated confidence through three primitives: choice(), score(), and noul().
Jev's choice() picks one option from a closed list and returns the pick, a probability distribution across all options, and a confidence.
Jev's score() rates something against a rubric the user describes, and GeoDeploy uses 10 levels.
Jev's noul() answers a yes/no question with a single probability.
Jev only ever selects from closed sets in GeoDeploy, never writes code or does arithmetic, so a hallucinated region like us-west-9 or a made-up Pulumi argument cannot happen by construction.
For each geo, GeoDeploy sends Jev a shortlist of up to 40 priced candidates along with the constraints and the image's architecture.

In a single call GeoDeploy asks Jev for a selection (choice), five quality scores (coverage, cost fit, maturity, sprawl risk, architecture consistency), two hard checks (noul: data residency satisfied, enough capacity), and a fallback (choice) region.
The GeoDeploy code at packages/decide/src/questions.ts imports choice, noul, and score from "@typesafe-ai/sdk" and builds the Stage A questions.
The rubrics follow TypeSafe's advice to "describe situations, not degrees."

Each of the 10 coverage levels is a concrete scenario, ranging from "Serves users on a different continent with no nearby presence" to "In-geo with multiple availability zones, directly in or adjacent to the demand geo's primary population center."

The TypeSafe SDK exposes a TypeSafeClient class whose systemOne method accepts state and questions and returns answers with fields such as selection.choice, selection.confidence, residencyOk.noul, and coverage.score.
GeoDeploy's ranking runs on weight profiles: latency-optimized (default), balanced, residency-first, and failure-domain, and weights live in code so ranking can be re-tuned without calling Jev again.

GeoDeploy's weight profiles are: latency-optimized {cost 0.13, coverage 0.48, maturity 0.17, sprawl 0.1, archConsistency 0.12}; balanced {0.25, 0.25, 0.2, 0.12, 0.18}; residency-first {0.12, 0.12, 0.38, 0.23, 0.15}; failure-domain {0.08, 0.17, 0.48, 0.15, 0.12}.
In GeoDeploy's composite ranking, sprawl risk is subtracted because every extra cloud provider means more credentials, tooling, and on-call runbooks.
In GeoDeploy, cluster and registry modules follow directly from the provider (AWS always means EKS and ECR), and Jev decides only ingress posture, autoscaling posture, and node-pool sizing tier.

GeoDeploy's confidence gate thresholds are: data residency 0.95 (hard reject); region for a new cluster 0.90 (top three candidates flagged for human choice); region when a stack already exists 0.75 (keep existing region); ingress or autoscaling module 0.85 (use registry default); node-pool sizing tier 0.60 (use bin-packing result); global floor for region pick, residency, or capacity 0.50 (drop the AI path for that geo).

GeoDeploy's residency check in packages/decide/src/engine.ts hard-rejects (throws AiPathAborted) when residencyOk confidence is below GATE_THRESHOLDS.residencyOk, and also throws if the model selects a candidate id not in the shortlist.
Each AiPathAborted in GeoDeploy carries the full attempt (state, questions, and answers), so even rejected answers end up in the audit trail.

If a gate check fails, the API times out or errors, or the upstream is unreachable, GeoDeploy switches to a deterministic fallback that compares prices across providers while still enforcing residency and constraint checks.
The `geodeploy explain` command shows why each region won.

When self-driving mode is enabled with `geodeploy monitor`, GeoDeploy periodically checks each deployment's CPU utilization and asks Jev one joint question across all regions with options no-change, scale-up:<geo>, scale-down:<geo>, or shift:<from>-><to>, plus a separate disruption-risk check.
In GeoDeploy self-driving mode, code (not Jev) computes the actual node-count changes.

In GeoDeploy self-driving mode, above 0.85 confidence the resize is applied automatically; between 0.70 and 0.85 it is suggested for human approval; below 0.70 GeoDeploy ignores Jev's pick and falls back to a deterministic per-region rule based on observed utilization.
CPU utilization alone makes a poor autoscaling metric and is usually paired with other signals such as median end-to-end request latency and error rates once a traffic baseline is established.
GeoDeploy is released as open source and can be used with access to Jev and a cloud provider.
GeoDeploy picks the best AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud region for users, gates every AI decision on confidence, and provisions Kubernetes.
GeoDeploy asks Jev to pick the best region per geo from a closed list so it cannot hallucinate a region.
GeoDeploy gates every decision on confidence, with hard rejects for data residency.
GeoDeploy provisions consistent clusters with one Pulumi stack per region.
GeoDeploy scales itself in self-driving mode, with a human in the loop when confidence is low.
The link /docs/iac/automation-api/ is a valid Pulumi docs page for the Automation API.
https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction is the TypeSafe Jev documentation page.
